evals.prompt: Northvale Systems - we sell a mid-market ITSM platform, $48k ACV. Average sales cycle from opportunity creation to closed-won is 140 days. I'm writing our first deal-registration policy for our four reseller partners. My draft was going to be: 30-day protection window (that's what our biggest competitor publishes), approval "as fast as we reasonably can", and rejections handled case by case by whoever picks up the form. Registration grants price protection, nothing else. Write the policy.
evals.expected_output: A deal-registration policy that resizes the protection window against the reported 140-day cycle, replaces the vague approval promise with a named SLA, publishes a closed list of objectively verifiable rejection grounds, and adds a non-price support bundle to what registration grants.
expectations: States the rule that the protection window must be at least 75% of the average sales-cycle length
Recommends a protection window of at least 105 days and explicitly rejects the proposed 30-day window
Derives the window recommendation from the stated 140-day cycle rather than citing a bare standard number
Defines an extension rule with a defined length and a documented-activity trigger, rather than leaving the window open-ended
Replaces "as fast as we reasonably can" with a named approval SLA, defaulting to 48 hours
Keeps registration approval and dispute adjudication as two separate clocks with two different durations
Sets the dispute-adjudication SLA at 5 business days
Publishes rejection grounds as a closed, explicit list instead of case-by-case approver discretion
Makes every listed rejection ground objectively verifiable from the registration record, with none left discretionary
Names duplicate registration or an account already in the active direct pipeline as a rejection ground
Names insufficient proof of partner involvement or value-add, a "just forwarding a name" submission, as a rejection ground
Adds a non-price support bundle such as pre-sales engineering access, priority deal support, or co-marketing support to what registration grants, rather than price protection alone
Warns that slow or ad-hoc approval is itself what drives speculative land-grab and duplicate registrations

evals.prompt: Kestrel Data, B2B analytics, roughly $60k ACV, 22 quota-carrying AEs. Our VP of Direct Sales has volunteered to approve all partner deal registrations since he knows every account in the pipeline better than anyone. Partnerships would own and publish the partner-influenced revenue number each quarter, and he and my partner manager would settle any credit arguments between themselves when they come up. Write the decision-rights section of our co-sell charter.
evals.expected_output: A decision-rights section that moves registration approval off the VP of Direct Sales on separation-of-powers grounds, co-owns attribution with revenue operations, and replaces ad-hoc credit negotiation with a named adjudicator, an SLA and a timestamp tiebreaker.
expectations: Rejects the VP of Direct Sales as registration approver because the approver's own quota must not be affected by the decision
Reassigns registration approval to partnerships or channel/partner operations, a function with no competing quota
Frames the problem as a structural conflict of interest rather than a question of trusting the individual
Assigns first-pass duplicate and territory-conflict review to channel operations
Retains an administrator override path to reverse mistaken approval or rejection decisions
Rejects partnerships as sole owner of the partner-influenced revenue number
Makes attribution co-owned by partnerships and revenue operations
Justifies co-ownership as making the number an auditable company fact rather than a self-serving one
Replaces case-by-case dispute settlement between two people with a named adjudicator and a defined SLA
Sets the dispute-adjudication SLA at 5 business days
Names the timestamped registration record as the objective tiebreaker in contested credit
Names a specific role on every decision-rights line rather than a team or shared ownership

Flags rules-of-engagement document ownership - partner or ecosystem leadership, co-designed with sales, CS, RevOps and legal - as a practitioner convention the user must confirm for their own org, not a measured industry standard

evals.prompt: Tuppence, two founders, seed stage. We sell a $29/month scheduling tool, self-serve signup, no sales team - our biggest account pays $1,400 a year. We're not growing as fast as we'd like and a channel seems like the obvious unlock. Build us the full co-sell operating charter: registration policy, deal credit splits, rules of engagement, the lot. We want resellers and SIs.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to build the charter, with the disqualifiers named explicitly, and a recommendation to run two or three deeply engaged referral partners with no formal program instead.
expectations: Declines to produce the co-sell operating charter rather than drafting it as asked
States the reasons for declining explicitly instead of declining vaguely
Names the ACV floor of roughly $3,000-$5,000 for any sales-assisted motion and places the stated $1,400 annual contract value below it
Flags the absence of a proven direct sales motion as a disqualifier, stating that partners amplify a working direct motion and do not fix a broken one
Identifies reaching for partnerships as a fix for a growth problem as itself a disqualifier, given the stated slow-growth motivation
Recommends two or three deeply engaged referral partners with no formal program as the alternative
Declines to design reseller or SI mechanics at this stage
Produces no protection window, no deal-credit split, and no comp-neutrality model
Notes that a trivially cheap, self-serve, auto-installing product may structurally have no partner play at all regardless of stage
States what would have to change before the readiness gate could be revisited
Notes that a formal program with a dedicated full-time operator only pays off around the EUR 1M-5M ARR range, and that a part-time owner below that is inadequate

evals.prompt: Halberd Cloud. We're standing up one registration policy that covers everybody: 6 resellers, 2 distributors, 4 SI/consultancy partners, 9 ISVs with integrations into our platform, and about 30 referral partners, mostly ex-customers who send us intros. Plan is one form, one 10% registration discount for all of them, one 60-day window. Keeps it simple and nobody can claim favouritism. Sanity-check it.
evals.expected_output: A rejection of the single undifferentiated policy, with each partner type mapped to the mechanic its own economics require, and the registration discount deleted outright for the types that do not earn on margin.
expectations: Rejects a single undifferentiated registration policy applied across all partner types
Maps each named partner type to the registration and credit mechanic its own economics require
States that referral partners need clean attribution and payment reliability, not margin protection or formal registration
States that resellers and distributors need formal deal registration, with distributors at the same formal tier plus reseller-network development tooling
States that SI/consultancy partners are motivated by services pipeline, certification and qualified leads, and that resale-style registration does not map to them
States that ISV/tech partners need integration certification, marketplace listing or developer access, and that resale registration is commercially irrelevant to them
Deletes the registration discount from the menu for the SI, ISV and referral partners rather than offering them a reduced rate
Justifies that deletion on the ground that those types do not earn on margin, so a discount buys no registration behaviour at any level
Keeps the discount as a live option only for the resellers and distributors, where margin is their economics
Recommends a non-price bundle - pre-sales engineering access, priority deal support, co-marketing support - as the default grant
States the ordering of the two grant types explicitly and notes that it inverts for resellers and distributors
Notes that a published discount is effectively irreversible once granted to the channel while a non-price bundle stays adjustable per partner
Flags that one identical policy in the name of fairness produces a policy that motivates no partner type correctly

evals.prompt: Ardent Logistics Software, enterprise, $180k ACV. Our CRO told me flatly that the comp plan is locked until the FY27 planning cycle 14 months out and he will not reopen it - not for this, not for anything. Meanwhile our 3% marketplace fee currently comes out of the AE's commission, and AEs lose 40% of quota credit on any deal a reseller touches. I have about 20 hours over the next month and I need something I can actually ship this quarter. What's the plan?
evals.expected_output: A plan that deletes every comp-neutrality funding rung outright because the comp plan is closed, records the missing neutrality as a stated known risk, and caps the deliverable at the registration and rules-of-engagement work that fits within the quarter.
expectations: Deletes all three comp-neutrality funding models from the plan rather than demoting or deferring them
Names the CRO's refusal to reopen the comp plan as the specific answer that deleted them
Records the missing comp neutrality as a stated known risk rather than an item at the bottom of a to-do list
Explains that a rung parked at the bottom of a list silently reappears later as scope nobody can sign
Caps the deliverable at registration policy and rules of engagement
Identifies the 40% quota-credit loss and the 3% marketplace fee passed to commission as the canonical adoption killer behind reps routing around or sandbagging partner deals
States plainly that the sandbagging behaviour will persist while comp is untouchable, rather than implying the remaining fixes resolve it
Promotes the one-hour, partnerships-only fixes - published rejection grounds, and the attribution lock window plus dispute SLA - given the within-quarter deadline
Deletes the heavyweight joint-business-planning track given the within-quarter deadline
Expresses effort as hours, meetings, sign-off chains and reversibility, never as a currency amount
States the ranking of the remaining fixes out loud with an explicit ordering line rather than implying it by list order
Does not propose full double comp, quota retirement or a secondary channel metric as a phased or later-stage recommendation

evals.prompt: Meridian Fielding, HR tech, $55k ACV, 90-day cycle. Co-sell has been live 18 months. Where we're at: rejection grounds have been published for over a year, registrations show up as a field on the opportunity record in the CRM so AEs see them there, and attribution locks two weeks after deal creation with a 5-day dispute SLA. Despite all of that our AEs still quietly drag their feet on partner deals - three partner managers have complained this quarter. Give me the remediation plan, ordered.
evals.expected_output: A remediation plan that promotes comp neutrality to first position because the exact promotion symptom is present, names the default ordering it overrides, and does not re-recommend the three fixes already in place.
expectations: Promotes comp neutrality to the first fix rather than the last
Names the promotion trigger explicitly: reps still sandbagging or routing around partner deals after registration visibility, published rejection grounds and the lock window are all already in place
States that the default efficiency ordering ranks comp neutrality last and that this case overrides the default
Does not re-recommend published rejection grounds, registration visibility, or the lock window plus dispute SLA as new work, since all three are reported as already in place
Emits separate ordering lines for efficiency and for value where the two axes disagree
States that comp neutrality is the highest-value fix and the worst ratio, and gives the reason: a contractual commitment to the field, a quarter of work, and a finance-plus-CRO sign-off chain
Warns that following the efficiency line alone means working the cheap rungs forever and never buying the one fix the others cannot substitute for
Checks whether quota credit shrinks when a partner attaches, or a marketplace fee hits commission, as the diagnostic behind the reported symptom
Recommends quota retirement as the default comp-neutrality rung, on the ground that it is one clause, one sign-off chain, and reversible at the next plan cycle
Names full double comp as the move-up option and ties it to this symptom persisting after quota retirement is already in place
States the required sign-off chain: finance funds the parity, and sales leadership or the CRO embeds it in the comp plan and the rules-of-engagement document
Warns that executive buy-in to alter field comp is difficult in practice and needs real political effort budgeted for it
Expresses fix effort in orders of magnitude such as an hour, a week or a quarter, never as a currency amount

evals.prompt: Sablefield, dev-tools vendor, $75k ACV. Today, at the end of each quarter, my partnerships team goes through the closed-won list and tags the deals a partner helped with. Sales does not trust the number and keeps saying we're marking our own homework. Separately, we just lost three weeks on one deal where a hyperscaler rep, a regional SI and one of our own referral partners all claimed a piece of it - our registration tool only has a single partner field per opportunity. Fix the attribution section of our charter.
evals.expected_output: An attribution section that moves the claim upstream of the outcome with a 14-day lock after deal creation, co-owns the number with revenue operations, and writes an explicit multi-party split rule decided at registration.
expectations: Rejects credit claims made after the deal closes, on the ground that a claim made once the outcome is known is unprovable and political
Requires the attribution claim to exist before the outcome is known
Sets an attribution lock window of 14 days after deal creation
Explains that the lock window exists to prevent backdated or opportunistic late credit claims
Moves ownership of the number from partnerships alone to partnerships co-owned with revenue operations
States the partner-sourced test as "would the deal still exist if the partner had not participated?"
Distinguishes partner-sourced from partner-influenced and keeps them as separate records rather than one flag
Requires an explicit multi-party split rule written into the charter instead of assuming one partner per deal
States that the multi-party split is decided at registration, not at close
Cites the structural argument that a customer works with roughly seven partners in a typical buying process
Sets a monthly or quarterly reconciliation cadence for contested or ambiguous attribution
Names the deal-registration timestamp as the objective tiebreaker for contested attribution
Notes that most registration systems were built for one partner per deal, so the single-field limitation is a known structural problem in co-selling rather than a local tooling bug

evals.prompt: Corvid Analytics. The board wants one headline partner number each quarter - "partner-attached revenue" - and my CRO wants me to commit to hitting 40% partner-sourced pipeline by Q4 because he read that's where mature programs land. One partner, Ridgeway Consulting, is currently 48% of everything our channel does. Write the KPI section of our co-sell charter.
evals.expected_output: A KPI section that keeps sourced and influenced as separate tracked numbers, refuses the borrowed 40% target, flags the single-partner concentration, and confines win-rate and cycle comparison to the company's own data.
expectations: Recommends tracking partner-sourced and partner-influenced separately rather than reporting only a combined partner-attached number
Explains that a combined number cannot tell whether partners generate pipeline or accelerate it
Allows partner-attached only as an additional executive roll-up alongside the two separate numbers, never as a replacement for them
Refuses to commit to the 40% partner-sourced figure as a target, and flags the published 20-30% and 40-50% ranges as vendor content rather than independent research
Flags Ridgeway Consulting at 48% of channel revenue as concentration risk against a threshold of roughly 30%
Includes registration time-to-approval, dispute rate and adjudication-SLA compliance among the tracked KPIs
Includes attach rate among the tracked KPIs
States that no independent industry benchmark exists for registration approval rate or time-to-approval, so targets must come from the program's own history
Restricts win-rate and cycle-length comparison between partner-attached and direct deals to Corvid's own data
Explains that cross-company win-rate comparison is unreliable because opportunity-creation criteria differ by company
Sets a quarterly review cadence for the KPI set
Does not present the partner-lift trio of bigger deals, higher win rates and faster cycles as established fact

evals.prompt: Ambergate, security vendor. We're kicking off with Northcliff Integrators, a 400-person SI. Their partner team is keen but their leadership will not commit anyone at VP level to this - I've asked twice and got nothing back. I want to run a proper joint business plan with them: exec kickoff on both sides, shared objectives, quarterly reviews, the full thing. I also have 11 other smaller partners I'd eventually want to do the same with. How do I run the JBP?
evals.expected_output: A recommendation that removes the heavyweight JBP track from the menu because no partner-side executive sponsor exists, and runs the lightweight single-session playbook fill for Northcliff and the other 11 partners instead.
expectations: Removes the heavyweight joint-business-planning track from the menu entirely rather than presenting it and recommending against it
Names the missing partner-side executive sponsor as the reason for that deletion
States that an unsponsored joint plan produces a document nobody executes
Recommends the lightweight single-session playbook fill for Northcliff Integrators instead
Specifies the lightweight track as one fixed template filled per partner in a single 90-minute working session
Specifies that the template is built once and reused, with only the content changing per partner

Lists the template sections: ICP and target-account criteria, roles and ownership matrix, joint deal-stage map with an exit criterion per stage, messaging and assets per stage, and metrics and review cadence
Requires a named individual, never a team, in every cell of the ownership matrix
States "shared ownership is no ownership" as the reason for the named-individual rule
Makes the lightweight track the default for all 12 partners until something specific moves one of them up
States the condition that would move a partner up to the heavyweight track: needing to influence that partner's own quota-carrying field sellers, with both sides funding the review cadence
States the ordering across the two tracks on more than one axis and notes that value and efficiency disagree
Names a named executive sponsor appearing later as the trigger to revisit the heavyweight track

evals.prompt: Fennimore Systems. I'm putting the co-sell business case in front of our exec team next Tuesday. I want to open with the three stats everyone quotes - partner deals close faster, close bigger, and have the highest win rate of any channel - then position us on an ecosystem-led growth maturity model so they can see we're at stage 2 of 5. Draft the framing and tell me what numbers to put on the slide.
evals.expected_output: A framing that grades each borrowed claim honestly, corrects the win-rate stat, refuses the maturity-model placement, and substitutes a measurement plan built on Fennimore's own data.
expectations: Flags the partner-lift trio of bigger deals, higher win rates and faster cycles as tracing to vendor marketing rather than independent research
Corrects the "highest win rate" claim by noting the underlying data shows partner referrals have the highest sales velocity, roughly 3.8x, which is a different claim
Refuses to present the three stats as targets or commitments to the exec team
Attaches the vendor-sourced, directional-only flag to any of those figures that are still quoted at all
Refuses to place Fennimore at "stage 2 of 5" on a maturity model
States that co-sell readiness and maturity models are competing consultant frameworks with no canonical standard, and presents them as a category of options
Identifies "ecosystem-led growth" and "nearbound" as real but vendor-coined vocabulary, usable as shared language and never as doctrine

Separates what is safe to present prescriptively - the partner-sourced / partner-influenced / partner-attached taxonomy, comp neutrality, rules-of-engagement documents, and deal registration with protection windows - from what is not
Proposes a partner-attached versus direct comparison inside Fennimore's own data as the substitute for the borrowed statistics
Names the absence of any independent benchmark as the reason the borrowed figures cannot carry the business case
